items.stem: What is meant by the atmosphere?
items.answer: The blanket of air that surrounds the Earth
items.markingKey: 1 mark: The atmosphere – the blanket of air that surrounds the Earth.

items.stem: Why is the Earth the only planet in the solar system known to support life?
items.answer: It has liquid water, an atmosphere with oxygen, a suitable temperature range, and an ozone layer and magnetic field that protect from harmful radiation.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: water and air. 1 mark: suitable temperature/protection.

items.stem:
Assertion (A): Life exists on the Earth.
Reason (R): The Earth has liquid water, air and a suitable temperature.
Choose the correct option.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: (a) R explains A.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

items.stem: A classroom measures 5 m × 4 m × 3 m. About what volume of oxygen does the air in it contain? (Air is about 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen by volume.)
items.markingKey: Volume of room = 60 m³; oxygen = 21% of 60 = 12.6 m³.

items.stem: Imagine all the Earth's water is 500 litres. About 97% is salty sea water and about 3% is fresh water, of which about two-thirds is locked in ice and glaciers. How many litres of fresh water would be liquid and usable?
items.markingKey: Fresh water = 3% of 500 = 15 L; ice ≈ 2/3 of it = 10 L; liquid ≈ 5 L (about 1%).

items.stem: A classroom measures 5 m × 4 m × 3 m. About what volume of nitrogen does the air in it contain? (Air is about 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen by volume.)
items.markingKey: Volume of room = 60 m³; nitrogen = 78% of 60 = 46.8 m³.

items.stem: Which term is described here? "The region around a star where a planet can have liquid water on its surface."
items.markingKey: (b) The habitable zone is the region around a star where a planet can have liquid water on its surface.

items.stem: A classroom measures 10 m × 8 m × 4 m. About what volume of nitrogen does the air in it contain? (Air is about 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen by volume.)
items.markingKey: Volume of room = 320 m³; nitrogen = 78% of 320 = 249.6 m³.

items.stem:
Read: The air on the Earth is about 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, 0.9% argon and about 0.04% carbon dioxide. Mars has a thin air of about 95% carbon dioxide; its surface temperature can drop to −125 °C.
(i) Which gas do we breathe in for respiration? (ii) Why can humans not breathe on Mars? (iii) Mars has a lot of CO₂—why is it still so cold? (iv) Name one other feature that makes the Earth suitable for life.
items.answer: (i) Oxygen. (ii) There is hardly any oxygen. (iii) Its atmosphere is very thin and it is farther from the Sun, so little heat is trapped. (iv) Liquid water / ozone layer / suitable temperature.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each.

items.stem: If the Earth were as close to the Sun as Venus, predict two changes on the Earth and their effect on life.
items.answer: Temperatures would be much higher; oceans would evaporate and liquid water would be lost; more greenhouse gases would trap heat; most life could not survive.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per change with effect (max 3).

items.stem: A classroom measures 6 m × 5 m × 3 m. About what volume of oxygen does the air in it contain? (Air is about 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen by volume.)
items.markingKey: Volume of room = 90 m³; oxygen = 21% of 90 = 18.9 m³.

items.stem: Which layer of the atmosphere is the layer where auroras occur and the International Space Station orbits?
items.markingKey: (a) The thermosphere is the layer where auroras occur and the International Space Station orbits.

items.stem: Which layer of the atmosphere is the layer above the troposphere that contains the ozone layer, where jets fly?
items.markingKey: (d) The stratosphere is the layer above the troposphere that contains the ozone layer, where jets fly.

items.stem: Arrange these layers of the atmosphere from the Earth's surface upwards: mesosphere, thermosphere, stratosphere.
items.markingKey: Order from the ground: troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere, thermosphere, exosphere.

items.stem: Arrange these layers of the atmosphere from the Earth's surface upwards: exosphere, mesosphere, thermosphere, troposphere, stratosphere.
items.markingKey: Order from the ground: troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere, thermosphere, exosphere.

items.stem: Mount Everest is about 8.8 km high and the troposphere reaches about 12 km at the equator but only about 8 km at the poles. Why do climbers on Everest need oxygen cylinders even though they are still in the troposphere?
items.answer: Air becomes thinner with height, so each breath contains much less oxygen near the top of the troposphere, even though the gases are in the same proportion.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: air thinner with height. 1 mark: less oxygen per breath.

items.stem: Which layer of the Earth is the thin outermost solid layer on which we live?
items.markingKey: (c) The crust is the thin outermost solid layer on which we live.

items.stem: Which layer of the atmosphere is the lowest layer, where weather occurs and where we live?
items.markingKey: (d) The troposphere is the lowest layer, where weather occurs and where we live.

items.stem: Which layer of the atmosphere is the outermost layer that gradually merges into space?
items.markingKey: (c) The exosphere is the outermost layer that gradually merges into space.

items.stem: Arrange these layers of the atmosphere from the Earth's surface upwards: mesosphere, thermosphere, exosphere, troposphere, stratosphere.
items.markingKey: Order from the ground: troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere, thermosphere, exosphere.

items.stem: Why do aeroplanes prefer to fly in the lower stratosphere?
items.answer: There are almost no clouds or weather disturbances there, so the flight is smooth.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: no weather. 1 mark: smooth flight.

items.stem: Which layer of the atmosphere is the layer where auroras occur and the International Space Station orbits?
items.markingKey: (b) The thermosphere is the layer where auroras occur and the International Space Station orbits.

items.stem: What is meant by rainwater harvesting?
items.answer: Collecting and storing rainwater for later use or to recharge groundwater
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Rainwater harvesting – collecting and storing rainwater for later use or to recharge groundwater.

items.stem: Which of the following is an inexhaustible resource?
items.markingKey: (d) Tides is an inexhaustible resource. The others: coal – a non-renewable resource; mica – a non-renewable resource; iron ore – a non-renewable resource.

items.stem: Why is solar energy a good alternative to coal for producing electricity?
items.answer: Sunlight is inexhaustible and causes no air pollution, while coal is limited and pollutes.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: inexhaustible. 1 mark: clean.

items.stem: Which of the following is NOT a renewable resource?
items.markingKey: (d) Petroleum is a non-renewable resource, not a renewable resource. Each of the others (forests, fresh water, soil) is a renewable resource.

items.stem: Classify these resources as a renewable resource or an inexhaustible resource: wildlife, air, fish in the sea, wind.
items.answer: A renewable resource: fish in the sea, wildlife. An inexhaustible resource: air, wind.
items.markingKey: ½ mark per correctly placed item (rounded): A renewable resource: fish in the sea, wildlife. An inexhaustible resource: air, wind.

items.stem: A school roof in Pune has an area of 150 m² and the city receives 600 mm of rain in a year. About how many litres of rainwater could be harvested in a year? (1 m³ = 1000 L)
items.markingKey: Volume = area × rainfall = 150 m² × 0.6 m = 90 m³ = 90000 L.

items.stem:
Read: A school in Jaipur plans rooftop rainwater harvesting. The roof area is 120 m² and the yearly rainfall is 800 mm. The school uses about 3000 L of water a day.
(i) How much rainwater (in litres) can be collected in a year? (1 m² × 1 mm = 1 L) (ii) For about how many days would it meet the school's needs? (iii) Is rainwater a renewable resource? (iv) Give one way to use the water other than storing it in tanks.
items.answer: (i) 96000 L. (ii) About 32 days. (iii) Yes. (iv) Lead it into a recharge pit to raise the groundwater level.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each part.

items.stem: Suggest a five-point plan for your school to become "green", with the resource each point saves.
items.answer: Solar panels (electricity/coal); rainwater harvesting (water); compost pit for food waste (soil/landfill); no single-use plastics (petroleum, wildlife); tree planting and switching off unused lights (forests/electricity).
items.markingKey: 1 mark per point with resource (max 5).

items.stem: Which of the following is a renewable resource?
items.markingKey: (c) Fresh water is a renewable resource. The others: petroleum – a non-renewable resource; air – an inexhaustible resource; natural gas – a non-renewable resource.

items.stem:
Read: Ritu's school in Bhopal measured the water used in a week: 12 000 L for toilets, 4000 L for drinking and cooking, 6000 L for gardening and 2000 L lost in leaking taps.
(i) What is the total water used? (ii) What percentage is lost through leaks? (iii) Suggest two ways to cut the water used for toilets and gardening. (iv) Why is saving fresh water important?
items.answer: (i) 24 000 L. (ii) 2000/24 000 × 100 ≈ 8.3%. (iii) Use dual-flush cisterns, reuse RO waste water, drip irrigation, water in the evening (any two). (iv) Usable fresh water is only about 1% of the Earth's water and is limited.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each.

items.stem: Which of the following is NOT a renewable resource?
items.markingKey: (c) Natural gas is a non-renewable resource, not a renewable resource. Each of the others (wildlife, soil, fresh water) is a renewable resource.

items.stem: Classify these resources as an inexhaustible resource or a renewable resource: tides, fish in the sea, wildlife, wind.
items.answer: An inexhaustible resource: tides, wind. A renewable resource: fish in the sea, wildlife.
items.markingKey: ½ mark per correctly placed item (rounded): An inexhaustible resource: tides, wind. A renewable resource: fish in the sea, wildlife.

items.stem: Which of the following is a renewable resource?
items.markingKey: (b) Wildlife is a renewable resource. The others: mica – a non-renewable resource; iron ore – a non-renewable resource; petroleum – a non-renewable resource.

items.stem: Classify these resources as an inexhaustible resource or a non-renewable resource: iron ore, sunlight, wind, mica.
items.answer: An inexhaustible resource: sunlight, wind. A non-renewable resource: iron ore, mica.
items.markingKey: ½ mark per correctly placed item (rounded): An inexhaustible resource: sunlight, wind. A non-renewable resource: iron ore, mica.

items.stem: Which term is described here? "A resource that cannot be replaced once used up, or takes millions of years to form, such as coal."
items.markingKey: (c) A non-renewable resource is a resource that cannot be replaced once used up, or takes millions of years to form, such as coal.

items.stem:

items.stem: What is meant by climate change?
items.answer: A long-term change in the average weather of the Earth, now mainly caused by human activities
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Climate change – a long-term change in the average weather of the Earth, now mainly caused by human activities.

items.stem:
Assertion (A): Global warming is a threat to coastal areas.
Reason (R): Rising temperatures melt glaciers and raise the sea level.
Choose the correct option.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: (a) R explains A.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

items.stem: Suggest three things a class 8 student can do every day to reduce global warming.
items.answer: Switch off fans and lights when not needed; walk, cycle or use the school bus; avoid wasting food and plastics; plant and care for trees.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per action (max 3).

items.stem: Your colony in Delhi burns dry leaves every winter. Explain two harmful effects and suggest a better practice.
items.answer: Burning releases smoke, soot and CO₂, worsening air pollution and breathing problems and adding to global warming. Better: compost the leaves.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: two effects. 1 mark: alternative.

items.stem: Scientists say that the Earth's average temperature has risen by about 1 °C in the last 100 years. Why is even this small rise a concern?
items.answer: It melts glaciers and ice sheets, raises sea level, causes more heat waves, droughts and floods, and disturbs crops and wildlife.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per effect (max 3).

items.stem: Why is the Earth called a "Goldilocks planet"?
items.answer: It is at just the right distance from the Sun—not too hot, not too cold—so water can stay liquid.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: right distance. 1 mark: liquid water.

items.stem: Which term is described here? "The gradual rise in the average temperature of the Earth due to an increase in greenhouse gases."
items.markingKey: (c) Global warming is the gradual rise in the average temperature of the Earth due to an increase in greenhouse gases.

items.answer: Meteors entering the atmosphere burn up due to friction with air, mostly in the mesosphere, and glow.
